---
title: "Closing and archiving the project"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

After submission, there are still files to archive, accounts to transfer and unfinished papers to discuss. Try to settle these while you can still access the systems and the people who know the project.

Start with an inventory. Decide what must be kept, shared, transferred or disposed of, and who will look after it. Then ask the next custodian to use the handover instructions. If they cannot locate a key file or reproduce an output, you have found something to fix before your access ends.

## Decide who looks after the work next {#transfer-custody-evidence-and-unfinished-obligations}

Every important record, asset and continuing obligation needs a destination and a responsible person. Give the recipient time to test access and recovery before closing your accounts.

You can also use this review to choose what you want to continue after candidature. A paper, collaboration or new question needs its own agreement, time and resources.

## Decide what “closed” means

List everything that belongs to the project:

- approved protocols, registrations and amendments;
- consent and participant-facing materials;
- source, working, analysis, publication and archival data states;
- metadata, dictionaries, provenance and quality records;
- code, software, environments, models and automation;
- laboratory, field, creative or physical materials;
- decisions, deviations, incidents and risk records;
- contracts, licences, partner and community agreements;
- manuscripts, thesis, reports, presentations and public outputs;
- authorship, contribution and copyright records;
- accounts, repositories, services, domains, keys and credentials;
- equipment, funds and purchased resources;
- open corrections, publications, reporting and access requests; and
- complaints, safety, integrity or legal matters in their authorised processes.

The inventory should name the authoritative copy, current state, custodian, permitted access, retention/disposal rule and next action.

## Decide what to keep, transfer or dispose of {#choose-a-disposition-for-every-item}

| Disposition | Meaning | Evidence required |
|---|---|---|
| Retain | keep in an approved controlled location for the required period | authority, custodian, location, access and review/disposal date |
| Archive | preserve a stable final state for long-term recovery or citation | manifest, identifiers, metadata, format and integrity check |
| Publish/share | release under a defined access and licence arrangement | permission, de-identification/governance checks, repository receipt |
| Transfer | move custody or responsibility to a named authorised recipient | handover package, access test and acceptance |
| Continue | retain as an active obligation after candidature | owner, resources, timeline, agreements and review point |
| Dispose | destroy or delete through an authorised process | rule, approval, method and evidence of disposal |
| Restrict/embargo | preserve but limit access for stated reasons and period | authority, conditions, review/end date and contact |

Check retention and disposal requirements before acting. Some material must be preserved; other material must be removed under consent, agreements or applicable rules.

## Build an archive manifest

For each retained collection record:

- project and collection identifier;
- description and purpose;
- authoritative location;
- creator, custodian and responsible unit;
- file formats, size and structure;
- checksums or other integrity evidence;
- metadata and data dictionary;
- provenance and transformation workflow;
- software/environment and execution instructions;
- approvals, consent, agreements and permitted uses;
- sensitivity and access controls;
- retention, review and disposal date;
- licence, citation and persistent identifier where applicable;
- known limitations; and
- related publications and outputs.

The Australian research-data guide assigns responsibilities for managing, retaining, sharing and disposing of research data and information; local policy and project agreements determine the operative details [@nhmrc-data-guide]. Open is not the default for sensitive or governed material, and FAIR aims do not override consent, cultural authority or legal restriction.

## Test preservation and recovery

Test whether the archived material can be opened, understood and used. Try the following checks.

1. permissions with the intended future role;
2. representative files in their archival formats;
3. checksums after transfer;
4. restoration from backup or archive;
5. environment reconstruction or documented emulation limits;
6. one key analysis, figure or artefact;
7. links and persistent identifiers; and
8. a recipient's ability to interpret limitations and permitted use.

Record the test, result, discrepancies and repair. If software or hardware cannot be preserved, retain sufficient documentation, formats and migration plan to make the limitation explicit.

## Hand over responsibility as well as access

A recipient needs:

- purpose and boundary;
- inventory and authoritative locations;
- current state and accepted outputs;
- decisions, deviations and unresolved questions;
- operation and recovery instructions;
- permissions, credentials route and restrictions;
- continuing obligations and deadlines;
- known risks and limitations;
- owner after transfer; and
- acceptance test.

Do not send passwords or personal tokens. Transfer service ownership through the supported process, create role-based access and remove personal access only after continuity is verified.

::: {.decision-card}
**Smallest useful next action:** Ask the future custodian to locate the approved input, recover one key output and explain one reuse restriction using only the handover package.
:::

## Close accounts and security exposure

Inventory institutional email, cloud storage, repositories, survey platforms, analysis environments, APIs, domains, equipment and shared services. For each:

- identify service owner and billing;
- export or transfer required records;
- rotate or revoke keys and tokens;
- remove departed users and excess permissions;
- preserve logs or audit evidence where required;
- verify shared automation still works;
- redirect essential contact routes; and
- close the account only after authorised acceptance.

Do not leave a shared project dependent on a personal email, payment card, multi-factor device or private repository.

## Reconcile outputs and continuing obligations

Create an output register for the following work.

- submitted, accepted, published and abandoned manuscripts;
- reviewer or examiner corrections;
- data/code/software releases;
- partner, community and funder reports;
- repository deposits and embargo reviews;
- authorship and corresponding-author responsibility;
- post-publication monitoring and correction; and
- enquiries or access requests.

Each continuing item needs an owner, authority, due/review date, contact path and evidence of completion. Graduation does not automatically terminate publication ethics, confidentiality, data stewardship or correction responsibilities.

## Example: “everything is in Dropbox”

The new custodian can see the folder but cannot identify the approved dataset, distinguish current from superseded analysis, restore the software environment or tell whether participant quotations may be reused.

Create a manifest, tag the final code release and record the source-data checksum and approved location. Add environment and execution instructions, link the consent and governance conditions, separate superseded outputs and assign continuing publication work.

The recipient tries a clean reproduction of Figure 3 and records any problems. Once the handover works, record acceptance, remove personal access and schedule retention and disposal dates. Keep unresolved items assigned in the continuing-obligations register.

## Decide what continues after candidature

Review four areas together:

- Which findings, methods or resources are worth extending, and which questions are finished or disproven?
- Which decisions can you now lead, and where would further training or collaboration help?
- Which research relationships have a continuing purpose, and which roles need renegotiating?
- Which papers, roles, fellowships or studies fit the available time, resources and permissions?

Choose among opportunities by considering their audience, contribution, timing and cost, including what each would displace. You do not need to carry every unfinished idea into the next role.

## Create a 90-day transition plan

Choose a small set of outcomes:

- close or transfer remaining candidature obligations;
- update professional records with verified rather than anticipated outcomes;
- communicate the thesis contribution to defined audiences;
- secure legitimate access and agreements for continuing work;
- select one or two next research questions;
- protect recovery after an intensive completion period; and
- establish the new project's governance and data plan before work begins.

The plan should distinguish accepted position, submitted application, invited discussion and aspiration. Completion of a doctorate changes capability and credentials; it does not make uncertain opportunities confirmed.


For career conversations and practical prompts, see [life during a PhD](../../stuck/life-during-a-phd.qmd#careers).

[]{#planning-work-beyond-the-doctorate}

## Complete the handover together

Ask the recipient to locate the research record, recover a representative output and explain any restrictions on reuse. Record their acceptance and unresolved items. Remove personal access only after the transfer works, and keep continuing papers, corrections and reports assigned to someone.

Take unresolved retention, ownership or access questions to the appropriate custodian before deleting or releasing material. For your own transition, choose a few achievable outcomes for the next 90 days and leave room to recover after completion.
